title: Recall-Aware Early Termination in Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search

problem.claim: Large-scale vector retrieval systems need high recall under strict latency constraints.

gap.claim: Fixed search parameters require substantial use-case-specific tuning and can over-search easy queries while under-searching hard queries because query difficulty and data distributions vary.

contributions.claim: An adaptive approximate nearest neighbor search framework incorporates user-specified recall requirements through early termination.
A learning-based mechanism predicts achieved recall during search and terminates early when the predicted recall reaches the target threshold.
A learning-based mechanism estimates the minimal candidate neighbor set size needed to satisfy user requirements and dynamically scales the candidate neighbor set.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The framework is index-agnostic and can be integrated into graph-based approximate nearest neighbor indexes, including HNSW, with negligible overhead.
Experiments on benchmark datasets and various graph indexes reportedly show significant query-latency reductions compared with state-of-the-art baselines.
The authors report that implementation code is publicly available.

narrative_sequence.summary: High recall under strict latency constraints is important for large-scale vector retrieval.
Existing fixed-parameter approaches require tuning and do not adapt well to heterogeneous query difficulty and data distributions.
The paper proposes recall-aware early termination with learning-based prediction of achieved recall and dynamic candidate neighbor set sizing.
The framework is presented as index-agnostic with negligible overhead, and experiments reportedly show lower query latency than state-of-the-art baselines.

source_observation.claim: Static search parameters can over-search easy queries and under-search hard queries.

interpretation.claim: Search effort may be better allocated through query-adaptive control tied to an explicit quality target.

application.claim: Systems with variable query difficulty could use predicted quality thresholds to stop or scale search dynamically.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether the approach generalizes beyond the reported graph-based approximate nearest neighbor indexes or how prediction errors affect recall guarantees.

unknowns: Exact latency reductions and recall outcomes are not reported.
The benchmark datasets and graph indexes are not identified.
The learning mechanisms, training procedure, prediction accuracy, and overhead measurement are not described.
Recall guarantees and behavior on difficult or distribution-shifted queries are not specified.
